sections.title: What a translator invoice must show
sections.body: A professional translation invoice needs specific details to pass an agency accounting department. Always include your purchase order number, the project name, and the exact language pair. You must clearly state the document name and the delivery date. If you use our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator, you can easily add these details in the description fields. Agencies process hundreds of invoices monthly, so missing a PO number often means a delayed payment. Make sure your tax registration details are visible if you are required to charge tax in your jurisdiction.
items: The exact language pair and direction of translation
The agency purchase order or project reference number
The specific file names of the translated documents
Your tax registration number if applicable to you

sections.title: How translator work is usually priced
sections.body: Translators use several pricing models depending on the text type. The most common method is a per-word rate. You must specify whether this applies to the source text or the target text, as word counts change dramatically between languages. Literary or creative translation might be billed per page or per hour, as word counts do not reflect the research involved. You will also need line items for urgency loading when working weekends. If you use translation memory software, clients expect repetition discounts for fuzzy matches, which you should itemise clearly.
items: Per-word rates based on source or target counts
Hourly rates for transcreation or complex formatting work
Minimum charges to cover small, low-word-count requests
Percentage additions for urgent or weekend delivery times

sections.title: Payment terms, deposits and chasing payments
sections.body: Translation agencies typically operate on standard thirty-day or sixty-day payment terms. Direct clients, however, might pay on receipt. For large projects spanning several weeks, it is wise to request a deposit before you begin translating. This secures your time and reduces risk. Clearly state your payment terms, bank details, and accepted payment methods at the bottom of the document. If a payment is late, send a polite reminder referencing the original project number. Keeping your billing organised helps you spot overdue accounts before you accept new assignments from that client.
items: Clear payment terms agreed before the translation begins
Upfront deposits for large or long-term translation projects
Complete bank details including international routing codes
Polite follow-up schedules for overdue agency payments

faqs.q: Should I charge by the source word or target word?
faqs.a: Charging by the source word is generally safer and more common in the translation industry. It allows you to give the client a fixed, exact quote before you even start working. Target word counts are completely unknown until the translation is finished. This uncertainty can lead to budget disputes if the final text expands significantly, which often happens when translating from English to languages like French or Arabic.

faqs.q: How do I show translation memory discounts on an invoice?
faqs.a: When using translation memory software, you will receive an analysis report showing exact matches, fuzzy matches, and new words. You should list the new words at your full rate. Then, add separate line items for the fuzzy matches and repetitions, applying the agreed percentage discount to each category. This transparency builds trust with agency clients.

faqs.q: What is a minimum charge and when should I use it?
faqs.a: A minimum charge is a flat fee applied to very small translation tasks, such as a single certificate or a short email. Even a fifty-word text requires you to read the brief, open your software, translate, proofread, and issue an invoice. A minimum charge ensures you are compensated for this administrative time, rather than earning just a few cents for the word count.

faqs.q: How do I bill for certified or sworn translations?
faqs.a: Certified translations often require physical stamping, signatures, or mailing hard copies to the client. You should charge your standard per-word or per-page rate for the translation work itself. Then, add a separate flat-fee line item for the certification process, and another line item to cover any courier or registered postage costs if physical delivery is required.
